senses: A person or business that provides customization services
ety: From customize + -er.
examples: Father Juliano declared bankruptcy after building only the prototype, but the car was restored a few years ago by a customizer in England.

senses: Concealing cover, disguise, veil; (also figurative).
Shelter, hiding place.
ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French coverture, from covrir (“to cover”) or from Late Latin coopertura. Doublet of couverture.
examples: URSULA. The pleasant'st angling is to see the fish Cut with her golden oars the silver stream, And greedily devour the treacherous bait: So angle we for Beatrice; who even now Is couched in the woodbine coverture.

senses: A man having physical characteristics of a cat.
ety: From cat + man.

senses: One who, or that which, aligns.
A thin flexible orthodontic tool that is fitted over the teeth to move them gradually.
ety: From align + -er.

senses: Elderly, old.
ety: From geriatrics. By surface analysis, Ancient Greek γῆρας (gêras, “old age”) + -iatric.

senses: Inclined or prone to fight.
ety: From Middle English fighti, figti, equivalent to fight + -y.

senses: self-sufficient
ety: From autarch(y) + -ic.

senses: One who, or that which, hinders.
ety: From Middle English hinderer, hindrere, hyndrer, hyndrere; equivalent to hinder + -er.

senses: The oceanic whitetip shark, Carcharhinus longimanus.
The whitetip reef shark, Triaenodon obesus.
ety: From white + tip.

senses: A decorative basket for the display of flowers or fruits.
ety: From French corbeil, from Latin corbicula, from corbis (“a basket”). Doublet of corbicula. By surface analysis, Latin corb- + -eil (“diminutive suffix”).

senses: One who, or that which, replies.
ety: From reply + -er.

senses: A three-stringed instrument of Okinawan origin, the precursor to the shamisen.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 三線 (sanshin) or Okinawan 三線 (sanshin, literally “three strings”). Doublet of sanxian.

senses: One who has a paraphilia.
ety: From paraphilia + -ic.

senses: Involving casual sexual intercourse.
ety: By surface analysis, ball + -ing.
examples: Ideal for a balling hot time .
And as Doran said later, all bullshit aside, what balling broad could resist going to bed with a handsome dwarf ?

senses: Having been subjected to peating.
ety: From peat + -ed.

senses: A 25-minute time interval spent working (followed by a five-minute break), used as part of the Pomodoro time management system.
ety: From Italian pomodoro (“tomato”). The time interval comes from the Pomodoro kitchen timer, which is in the shape of a tomato.
examples: If each pair works on 10 pomodoros per day, the total team capacity is 30 pomodoros per day.
Break the task down into 25-minute dashes (pomodoros). How many pomodoros do you think you'll need to complete the activity?

senses: Tabernanthe iboga, a perennial rainforest shrub and a source of the hallucinogen ibogaine.
ety: From Myene iboga.
examples: The powdered bark (especially the root bark) of the iboga shrub is consumed by the natives of Gabon and part of the Congo in the initiation rites of a number of secret societies.

Under the influence of iboga, the Bwiti initiates are able to communicate directly with an assembly of dead ones—a chain of ancestors. The initiate falls to the ground in a stupor after drinking the iboga brew.

senses: The action of being pushed or drawn beneath another object.
The act of subducting or taking away.
Arithmetical subtraction.
ety: From Latin subductiō, from subdūcere (“to draw from under or below”). Equivalent to subduct + -ion or subduce + -tion.

senses: Any eukaryote that exhibits amoeboid movement, having the ability to change its shape.
Any member of the class or phylum Sarcodina, a polyphyletic grouping into which diverse amoeboids were placed.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀμοιβή (amoibḗ, “change”), referring to constantly changing shape of these organisms.

senses: Occurring once every two months
Occurring twice every month.
ety: From bi- + monthly.
examples: The organization's bimonthly meetings allow for two discussions each quarter.
His bimonthly appointment was almost due.

senses: The fact or state of being for sale, especially with reference to bribes or corruption.
ety: From venal + -ity, from French vénalité or Latin vēnālitās, from vēnālis (“venal”), from vēnum; compare English vend.

senses: A human tower formed in festivals in Catalonia.
ety: Borrowed from Catalan castell. Doublet of cashel, castellum, castle, and château.

senses: A form of decorative extruded pasta.
ety: From Italian fiori (literally “flowers”).

senses: A forked tool used by clothiers for dressing cloth.
ety: From Middle English pren, from Old English prēon, from Proto-Germanic *preunaz (compare Icelandic prjónn (“pin, knitting-needle”), Danish pryne (“needle, eel-spear”)), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *brewn- (“protrusion, tip, edge”) (compare Lithuanian briaunà (“edge”), Albanian brez (“belt, girdle”)). Cognate with German Pfriem. The verb is from Middle English prenen, from pren (“a preen”), akin to German pfriemen.

senses: A polyploid organism.
ety: From poly- + -ploid.

senses: Characterized by assorting.
ety: From assort + -ative.
examples: Assortative interactions can generate highly nonrandom variation among groups.
We don’t date the girl next door; we date the girl who has been served up by an assortative algorithm.

senses: 3.7×10¹⁰ decays per second, as a unit of radioactivity. Symbol Ci.
ety: Borrowed from French curie. Named after French physicist Pierre Curie (1859–1906).

senses: A Japanese broth made from pork marrow, typically served with ramen.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 豚骨 (tonkotsu), from 豚 (ton, “pork”) + 骨 (kotsu, “bone, rib”).

senses: Especially, the common rhododendron or Pontic rhododendron (Rhododendron ponticum).
ety: The obsolete sense derives from Latin rhododendron (“oleander”), from Ancient Greek ῥοδόδενδρον (rhodódendron, “oleander”), from ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”) + δένδρον (déndron, “tree”). The modern sense comes through the intermediary of the genus name Rhododendron, not closely related taxonomically, but with similar flowers to those of oleander.

senses: Characterised by a hooting sound.
ety: From hoot + -y.
examples: Berg's partner here, Sophie Daneman, a young British soprano, has a small, pure, lyric voice that occasionally turns hooty (characteristic of many Britsh sopranos).
The hooty noise came again and this time seemed much closer.

senses: To specify each member of a sequence individually in incrementing order.
To determine the amount of.
ety: First attested in 1600–1650; borrowed from Latin enumerātus, the perfect passive participle of enumerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

senses: Datedness of something originally intended to seem futuristic.
ety: Coined by British science fiction writer and humorist Douglas Adams and British television producer and writer John Lloyd in The Meaning of Liff (1983), from Zeerust, the name of a town in South Africa. By folk etymology, connected semantics to rust.
examples: It also features a nice bit of Zeerust in the form of a carefully reproduced Hollerith card.

Sci-fi and futuristic- lots of potential here it seems to me, though not as many real world example rides as I expected. I wonder if it's a cost issue or a fear of getting zeerust setting in as the ride ages.

senses: Rapid flowering of a culture or civilisation etc.

An encrustation of soluble salts, commonly white, deposited on the surface of stone, brick, plaster, or mortar; usually caused by free alkalies leached from mortar or adjacent concrete as moisture moves through it.
ety: Borrowed from French efflorescence, from Latin efflōrēscō (from ex- (“out”) + flōrēscō (“to blossom”)) + -ence. By surface analysis, effloresce + -ence.

senses: Something that, or someone who, smashes.
A person employed to break up waste rock.
ety: From smash + -er.

senses: A large thing.
ety: Eye-dialect spelling of big 'un (one).

senses: A stand with a slanted top used to support a Bible from which passages are read during a church service.
A similar stand to support a lecturer's notes.
ety: 15th century partial re-Latinization of early 14th century Middle English lettorne, lettron, from Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lectus (from whence also lecture), form of Latin legō (“to read”).

senses: Any of certain fishes of the family Carangidae, especially of the genera Caranx and Pseudocaranx.
ety: Perhaps an alteration of cavally.

senses: One who theorizes or idealizes; one who advocates the doctrines of ideology.
ety: From ideology + -ist.
examples: In addition, the ruling thoughts of a particular era gradually become separate from the ruling individuals, i.e. intellectual labour becomes a distinct occupation and the profession of the ideologist is born.

senses: A storm spirit in Cornish folklore, traditionally believed to inhabit mines and coastal communities.
ety: Borrowed from Cornish bocka. Doublet of pooka and puck.

senses: To shoehorn, to cram.
ety: From Jemmy, diminutive of James. The verb is from the noun.
